Case study · Facebook · Settings & Controls

I shipped a four-year-stalled redesign to 3 billion users in four months.

Facebook's most-used control surface had become its least trusted: 14+ scattered options, and 44% of feedback calling it confusing. I led the redesign end-to-end and aligned the 10+ teams four years of attempts couldn't.

Simplified 14+ controls down to 4, shipped 1:1 as designed.
100% global rollout to 3B+ users.
+20% signal-quality improvement (NUF) from the UI alone.
Adapted mid-project to a Zuckerberg-requested Meta AI integration without losing the simplification goal.

3-dot menu · roadmap
01 · Overview

I owned Facebook's most-used control surface, end to end.

Sole designer on the 3-dot menu, across every Facebook surface. I partnered with one eng lead, data scientists, and 10+ cross-functional teams: Feed, Reels, Groups, Marketplace, Privacy, Integrity, and Risk.

02 · The problem

The most-used menu was also the least trusted.

Decision fatigue got so high and the business cost was real while competitors pulled ahead.

44%
of the words people used to describe the menu were negative: confusing, overwhelming, pushy.
03 · Context

Everyone had a stake. No one would give anything up.

10+ teams, all with something to lose, none willing to concede. It had been escalated and championed before, and still no one could get every team on the same page.

"Escalated, championed, and still stuck for four years. Until this."
04 · The process

I led with data, not design.

Before a pixel moved, I pitched two strategic options with honest tradeoffs and recommended the bold path. That set four principles for every decision after:

  • Only what matters
  • Instant clarity
  • Empowerment
  • Modern and YA-ready

With my eng lead, I built risk assessments and signal projections showing each team what the change meant for their numbers. Every control faced three questions: legally required? actually used? better housed elsewhere? Survivors: Interested / Not Interested, Save, Why am I seeing this, Report. Nothing was deleted, only rehomed, mapped control by control.

The two directions side by side, with the tradeoffs named. Radical was the recommendation, and the version leadership aligned on.
Options · decision artifact
The north star

Every control mapped to a job, and a tier.

Each control mapped to a job and a tier, the structure that decides what belongs in the menu and what lives one layer down.

05 · Systems thinking

A rule, so the menu never fills back up.

I set the bar for what comes next: unless a control moves a metric substantially or is legally required, it doesn't get in. Then I built the intake process to keep that structured, the part that stops the simplification from quietly unwinding.

06 · The curveball

Then Meta AI entered the chat.

Mid-process, Mark Zuckerberg asked for Meta AI to live in the menu, the opposite of the minimal model I'd been fighting for. I adapted without losing the goal: co-designing an AI Discovery Layer (summary, transparency, one-tap prompt entry) while holding the UI line on icon and token consistency.

That year I was ranked top 5 of 210 designers at Meta for AI-native practices, and it wasn't my first time building with AI as a first-class citizen. What shipped landed close to my original pitch.

The Meta AI layer
Discovery, without unwinding the work.
A generated summary and sourced links, opening from the top of the menu, added as a net-new surface while the four core controls stayed intact.
The same structure with the Meta AI discovery layer folded in: a net-new surface at the top, the four core controls left untouched.

07 · WHAT I WAS REACHING FOR

I took this on because it demanded a real voice at the table, not just execution. We held our own in rooms with leads four levels up, something four years of attempts couldn't.

07 · REFLECTION

The unlock wasn't a design decision, it was changing the conversation from design rationale to data, risk, and business impact. Great design at scale is the system that keeps the product healthy, not just the product itself.

Alignment is a design problem. I just happened to redraw a menu along the way.
